issues.legal_issue: The regulatory regime applies to ongoing real estate projects without a completion certificate, and that application is retroactive rather than impermissibly retrospective or unconstitutional.
material_facts: The law required ongoing projects without a completion certificate to be registered, while projects already completed or granted a completion certificate were outside its scope.
The projects at issue had been undertaken before the law came into force and did not have completion certificates.
The law regulated the projects’ future compliance and required promoters registering ongoing projects to set timelines for the remaining development work.
issues.conclusion: The law applies retroactively to ongoing projects without a completion certificate. This application does not violate Articles 14 or 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(1) and 3(2), read with Sections 13, 18(1) and 19(4), show the legislative intent to include ongoing projects without a completion certificate while excluding completed projects. A statute is not retrospective merely because some requisites for its operation arise from antecedent events; a retroactive statute operates in futuro based on an earlier character or status. The Court relied on State of Bombay (Now Maharashtra) v. Vishnu Ramchandra, Jay Mahakali Rolling Mills v. Union of India, Shanti Conductors Private Limited v. Assam State Electricity Board, and Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma. Parliament may legislate to cover pre-existing transactions and rights in the public interest, subject to constitutional limits.

rule.if: challenge_to_retroactive_application and ongoing_project and not completion_certificate and future_compliance_is_regulated

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_application: A party challenges the application of a regulatory law to a project begun before the law took effect.
predicates.ongoing_project: The project remained under development when the regulatory regime began to apply.
predicates.completion_certificate: The project had received a certificate confirming completion under the applicable requirements.
predicates.future_compliance_is_regulated: The law requires the promoter to comply with regulatory duties for the project after the law takes effect.

issues.definition: When a challenged law regulates future compliance for an ongoing project that has no completion certificate, its application is valid even though the project began earlier.

issues.legal_issue: The regulatory authority determines claims for refund and interest on refunded amounts, while the adjudicating officer determines claims for compensation and interest on compensation.
material_facts: Allottees complained that promoters had failed to hand over possession as agreed and sought repayment of the amounts invested with interest.
The authority directed refunds with interest after hearing the parties.
The Act distinguishes between return of the amount and compensation, and provides separate procedures for complaints to the authority and applications for compensation to the adjudicating officer.
issues.conclusion: The authority has jurisdiction to order a refund and interest on the refunded amount. The adjudicating officer has exclusive jurisdiction to adjudge compensation and interest on compensation under Sections 12, 14, 18 and 19.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18 and 19 establish an allottee’s right to return of the amount and interest, while Section 71 confines the adjudicating officer’s role to adjudging compensation; Section 72 provides factors relevant to that compensation determination. Section 31 permits complaints to the authority or adjudicating officer as appropriate. The Court also relied on the separate procedures in Rules 33 and 34 of the Uttar Pradesh Rules and Forms M and N. In Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni, the Court held that the allottee’s right to refund under Section 18 is unqualified when the promoter fails to give possession as agreed.

predicates.real_estate_regulatory_complaint: An aggrieved person brings a complaint under a real estate regulatory regime concerning a promoter’s conduct.
predicates.allottee_seeks_refund: An allottee asks to withdraw from the project and recover the amount paid.
predicates.promoter_failed_to_deliver_possession: The promoter failed to complete the project or deliver possession as agreed.

issues.definition: When an allottee brings a regulatory complaint seeking repayment after the promoter fails to deliver possession, the authority determines the refund and interest on it; a claim for compensation is determined separately by the adjudicating officer.

issues.legal_issue: A regulatory authority may delegate to one of its members the power to decide complaints, including refund complaints, when the governing law authorizes delegation and the delegation is made by written order.
material_facts: The authority made a written special order delegating the hearing and decision of complaints to a single member after a large volume of complaints had accumulated.
The single member heard the parties and decided complaints seeking refunds and interest.
The governing law expressly authorized the authority to delegate powers and functions to a member, subject to conditions, and excluded only the power to make regulations.
issues.conclusion: Delegation to a single member to decide complaints is permissible under the Act. The adjudicating officer’s powers under Section 71, however, cannot be delegated to a member or officer under that delegation power.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 21 and 29 address the authority’s composition and its meetings, including quorum for its business meetings; they do not prescribe a minimum bench strength for deciding complaints. Section 81 expressly permits written general or special delegation of the authority’s powers and functions, except its regulation-making power under Section 85. The Court relied on Saurashtra Kutch Stock Exchange Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India and Heinz India Private Limited v. State of Uttar Pradesh for the principle that statutory authorization makes such delegation permissible. It distinguished the adjudicating officer’s separate statutory role under Section 71, which is not delegable under Section 81.

predicates.complaint_decided_by_authority: An aggrieved person brings a complaint for decision by a regulatory authority.
predicates.statute_authorizes_delegation: The governing law permits the authority to delegate its powers or functions to a member.
predicates.written_delegation_to_member: The authority issues a written order assigning the complaint-deciding function to one of its members.

issues.definition: A member may decide a complaint for the authority when the law permits delegation and the authority assigns that function to the member by written order.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory pre-deposit condition imposed on a promoter seeking to appeal an order requiring payment to an allottee is a valid restriction on the right of appeal.
material_facts: Promoters challenged the requirement to deposit amounts before their appeals against orders directing payment to allottees could be entertained.
The orders could require payment of a refund, interest, compensation, or a penalty.
The statute imposed the pre-deposit condition on promoters, who were a distinct class from allottees and had separate rights, duties, and obligations under the regulatory scheme.
The condition was intended to safeguard amounts determined to be payable to allottees and to discourage unmeritorious appeals.
issues.conclusion: The pre-deposit condition for a promoter’s appeal is valid and is not discriminatory or an unreasonable restriction under Articles 14 or 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43(5) makes a promoter’s appeal subject to pre-deposit requirements, including where the order requires payment to an allottee. A statutory right of appeal is not an absolute right and may be made subject to conditions that are not so onerous as to make the right illusory. The Court found an intelligible differentia between promoters and allottees and considered the condition consistent with the Act’s aim of protecting consumers and preserving amounts determined to be payable. It relied on Narayan Chandra Ghosh v. UCO Bank, Har Devi Asnani v. State of Rajasthan, Government of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Laxmi Devi, Shreenath Corporation v. Consumer Education and Research Society, and Tecnimont Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab, among other decisions addressing statutory pre-deposit requirements.

rule.if: promoter_appeals_payment_order and appeal_requires_predeposit and distinct_promoter_obligations and predeposit_protects_awarded_amount

predicates.promoter_appeals_payment_order: A promoter appeals an order requiring payment to an allottee or imposing a penalty.
predicates.appeal_requires_predeposit: The governing appeal scheme requires the promoter to deposit an amount before the appeal can be heard.
predicates.distinct_promoter_obligations: The regulatory scheme places materially different rights, duties, and obligations on promoters and allottees.
predicates.predeposit_protects_awarded_amount: The deposit requirement is intended to preserve an amount determined to be payable and to deter unmeritorious appeals.

issues.definition: A pre-deposit requirement is valid where a promoter challenges a payment order, the parties have distinct regulatory roles, and the condition protects the amount determined to be payable.

issues.legal_issue: An amount determined to be refundable to an allottee, including the principal amount, is recoverable as arrears of land revenue when the promoter fails to pay it.
material_facts: The authority could direct promoters to refund the principal amount and pay interest to allottees.
The recovery provision expressly referred to interest, penalty, and compensation, but did not expressly mention the principal amount.
The Court found that treating the principal amount and interest as a composite quantified sum gave effect to the statutory scheme and its purpose of speedy recovery for allottees.
issues.conclusion: The amount determined to be refundable to an allottee by the authority or adjudicating officer is recoverable under Section 40(1), including the principal amount.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 authorizes the return of the amount paid, with interest, while Section 40(1) provides for recovery of specified sums as arrears of land revenue. The Court harmonized those provisions according to the purpose of the Act: allowing recovery only of interest while excluding the principal refund would defeat the statutory remedy and leave the allottee without an effective means to recover the amount invested.

predicates.refund_order_quantifies_amount_due: A competent decision-maker determines the amount that a promoter must refund to an allottee.
predicates.debtor_fails_to_pay: The person ordered to pay does not comply with the payment direction.
predicates.statutory_recovery_as_land_revenue_is_av: The governing law provides a process for recovering specified unpaid amounts as arrears of land revenue.

issues.definition: A quantified refund that remains unpaid can be recovered as arrears of land revenue when the governing law provides that recovery process.
